concept_html:
Bronze is your evidence. Its contract has four rules.

  1. Append only. Every delivery adds rows. Nothing in bronze is updated, deleted or overwritten. A redelivery of wave W14 appends again, with a new ingestion_id.
  2. As received. No cleaning, filtering, renaming or type casting. Read CSV columns as strings. inferSchema guesses types, and a guess can destroy data: the ID 00123 becomes the integer 123, and the leading zeros are gone for good.
  3. Audit columns. Add four columns to every row: ingestion_id (one UUID per load), source_file, ingestion_timestamp and delivery_version. Later layers use them to pick the newest version and to trace any number back to a file.
  4. Grain. One row per respondent per wave per delivery file. Duplicates across deliveries are expected here. Silver resolves them.

Why keep the mess? Because silver logic changes. When you fix a mapping bug in March, you rebuild silver from bronze for every wave since January. You can only do that if bronze still holds the original deliveries.

Two practical points for Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS:

  • Count what you wrote from the Delta history instead of calling count() before the write. DeltaTable.forName(spark, table).history(1) returns operationMetrics["numOutputRows"]. A separate count() reads the source file a second time.
  • Open-source Spark defaults saveAsTable to Parquet. Databricks defaults to Delta. Write .format("delta") explicitly, so the code behaves the same in local tests.

lines: import uuid
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
def add_audit_columns(df: DataFrame, ingestion_id: str, source_file: str, delivery_version: int) -> DataFrame:
"""Add the four bronze audit columns."""
return df.withColumns({
"ingestion_id": F.lit(ingestion_id),
"source_file": F.lit(source_file),
"ingestion_timestamp": F.current_timestamp(),
"delivery_version": F.lit(delivery_version),
})
def ingest_to_bronze(spark: SparkSession, path: str, table: str, delivery_version: int) -> int:
"""Append one delivery file to bronze as received. Returns rows written."""
raw = spark.read.option("header", True).csv(path)
audited = add_audit_columns(raw, str(uuid.uuid4()), path, delivery_version)
audited.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable(table)
metrics = DeltaTable.forName(spark, table).history(1).collect()[0]["operationMetrics"]
return int(metrics["numOutputRows"])

from pyspark.sql import DataFrame
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def add_audit_columns(df: DataFrame, ingestion_id: str, source_file: str, delivery_version: int) -> DataFrame:
    """Add the four bronze audit columns to a delivery.

    Args:
        df: The delivery as read, all columns as strings.
        ingestion_id: One UUID for this load.
        source_file: Path of the delivery file.
        delivery_version: Supplier's version number for the delivery.

    Returns:
        The delivery with ingestion_id, source_file, ingestion_timestamp and delivery_version.
    """
    return df.withColumns({
        "ingestion_id": F.lit(ingestion_id),
        "source_file": F.lit(source_file),
        "ingestion_timestamp": F.current_timestamp(),
        "delivery_version": F.lit(delivery_version),
    })

title: Bronze: keep every delivery exactly as received
why_html:
A bronze job reads supplier CSVs with inferSchema=true. Respondent IDs such as 00123 land as the integer 123. Months later, the supplier sends a correction file keyed on the original IDs, and 18% of rows fail to match silver. The original IDs are not recoverable from bronze, because bronze never held them. The team asks the supplier to resend six months of deliveries.

Reading every column as a string keeps 00123 intact. Silver can then cast deliberately, with checks.
